bib.title: Explaining Models: An Empirical Study of How Explanations Impact Fairness Judgment
bib.venue: IUI '19 (24th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces), Marina del Rey, CA

question: How do different styles of programmatically generated explanation affect people's judgment of the fairness of an ML system, and how do individual prior positions modulate that?
hypothesis: Local explanations, which justify a particular case, should surface fairness discrepancies between cases more effectively than global ones; sensitivity-based explanation should be most effective on raw (biased) data.
contributions: Four explanation styles generated automatically for the same data points from a real model
Between-subject test of data debiasing and within-subject test of case-specific disparate impact
Evidence that prior positions on ML and on the race feature change reactions to explanation styles
Qualitative themes on how people judge fairness and what they think of each style

method.summary: A logistic regression on COMPAS data (Caucasian and African-American defendants only) was trained on raw and on pre-processed (Calmon et al. 2017) data. Four explanation styles (input influence, demographic, sensitivity, case) were generated per prediction. 160 MTurk workers each rated the fairness of 6 predictions on a 1-7 scale, in a 2 (data) x 4 (style) between-subject design with disparate impact within-subject.
method.task: human fairness judgment of ML predictions under explanation (recidivism use case)

datasets.name: COMPAS recidivism data (Broward County, Florida, two-year span)
datasets.preprocessing: Only Caucasian and African-American kept; features age (5 bins), charge degree, prior convictions (5 bins), juvenile convictions, race; dummy coded with median category as reference; debiased variant via Calmon et al. 2017 optimized pre-processing

inference.samples: 6 trials per participant: 2 drawn from 8 disparately impacted cases, 4 from 16 non-impacted cases; 160 participants over 8 conditions
inference.retrieval: Case-based explanation: nearest-neighbour search in training data; shows % of identical training cases with the same label, or nearest neighbour if no exact match

parameters.disparate impact definition: flipping race changes prediction; 23 such cases in raw test data, all near boundary (mean confidence 52%, max 54%); processed classifier mean and max 50%

metrics.name: Fairness rating
metrics.definition: agreement with 'How the software made the prediction was fair', 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree)

metrics.name: Prior position scales (ML position, race position)
metrics.definition: mean of 5 bipolar adjective pairs on 7-point scale; Cronbach alpha 0.95 (ML) and 0.98 (race)

baselines: No no-explanation control; styles compared with each other and raw vs processed data
eval.protocol: Mixed-effects regression with F tests, p<0.05 significant and 0.05<=p<0.10 marginal; pairwise comparisons against a reference style; open-ended justification coded by the authors (open coding). Attention check after trial 3, all passed. Participants: US MTurk, >1000 tasks, >=98% approval, recruited September 2018; 62.5% male, 78.8% Caucasian, 29.4% under 30, 13.3% above 50. About 18 min, $3 each.

availability.data: Full explanation output in supplementary materials (referred to, no URL)

evidence.quote: 2 trials were randomly selected from the 8 disparately impacted cases, and 4 trials from the 16 non-impacted cases

results.claim: Disparate-impact cases were rated much less fair than others (main effect).
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression, base model
results.quote: significant main effect of disparate impact, F(1, 152) = 103.25, p < 0.001

results.claim: Debiased (processed) data raised fairness ratings (main effect).
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression, base model

results.claim: Style by disparate-impact interaction was only marginally significant in the base model.
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression, F(3,152)=2.35
results.quote: two-way interaction between explanation style and disparate impact, F(3, 152) = 2.35, p = 0.07

results.claim: Expected three-way interaction (style x data processing x disparate impact) was not significant in the base model.
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression
results.quote: The three-way interaction we expected is not significant, F(3, 152) = 0.54, p = 0.66

results.claim: Sensitivity vs influence pairwise contrast on the rating gap was significant.
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression, sensitivity as reference level
results.quote: influence-based explanation is significantly different, F(1, 156) = 5.14, p = 0.02

results.claim: Sensitivity vs demographic contrast was marginal.
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression, sensitivity as reference

results.claim: After adding race position and ML position, the three-way interaction became significant.
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression plus individual-difference terms
results.note: Printed text reads 'we now find the three-way interaction ... to be significant, F(3, 144) = 2.96, p = 0.03'; the quote is the fragment that occurs after a line break.

results.claim: A four-way interaction with race position was significant.
results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression, race_pos x style x data x impact

results.claim: Share of participants who considered using race fair or neutral.

results.setup: Mixed-effects regression (lmerTest, R), participant random effect, gender and race as covariates; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating; 160 MTurk workers, 6 trials each, COMPAS logistic regression plus individual differences
results.quote: main effect of ML position (F(1, 137) = 17.31, p < 0.001)

limits: Crowdworkers rather than judges, the actual users of such tools (Sec 8.3)
Many explanation styles and elements not studied; confidence deliberately not shown (Sec 8.3)
Key effects are marginal (p=0.07) and the expected three-way interaction only reached significance after adding individual-difference terms post hoc; no effect sizes reported
Measures perceived fairness, not detection of unfairness or decisions
One simple logistic regression on one 5-feature dataset with two racial groups
Need for cognition measured with 4 items only, for time
